title: Housing and homelessness actions and responses
subtitle: Four-unit zoning, daytime shelter, encampment wellness checks, winter planning and a housing reserve proposal referred to budget.
overview: Council met in a special session on housing and homelessness. A closed session came first. The mayor reported publicly that council only received information and gave no direction. In open session, council heard from staff and six delegates, then approved a package of staff recommendations {{vote:m5}}.

The package adopts a human rights-based approach to housing. It also orders a review of how the City and the County of Wellington govern social services, and it backs a County housing and homelessness symposium no later than the first quarter of 2024. Other items include advocacy letters to the province and a zoning amendment to allow up to four units per lot. Staff will report back by November on daytime shelter options and will work with Royal City Mission on a month-to-month extension of its current agreement.

Council added several requests. The County is asked to report on winter plans for homelessness and to lead wellness checks at encampments. Staff will also talk with the Guelph Community Health Centre about expanding Welcoming Streets. A proposed $1.5M for the Affordable Housing Reserve goes to the multi-year budget. Temporary encampments go to the County symposium. Residents should watch the November budget and shelter reports.

decisions.detail: Council approved the amended set of staff recommendations, including a human rights-based, Housing First approach, a governance review with the County, advocacy to other governments, a Housing Accelerator Fund plan, and a Royal City Mission extension review {{vote:m5}}.

decisions.item: Up to four units per lot
decisions.detail: Staff must promptly prepare a zoning by-law amendment allowing up to four residential units per lot where the new zoning by-law allows three, subject to servicing capacity.

Staff will seek feedback from downtown groups and the County on location and delivery of a 12-hour, seven-day daytime shelter, with the downtown-area limit removed, and report by November 2023 {{vote:m4}}.
Staff will start talks with the Guelph Community Health Centre on expanding Welcoming Streets and report back for the 2024 budget discussion {{vote:m6}}.
Council asked the County to share its plans and oversight for winter homelessness, including warming centres and any need for more shelter, through an upcoming information report {{vote:m7}}.
A proposal to budget $1.5M for the Affordable Housing Reserve was referred to the 2024-2027 multi-year budget process {{vote:m9}}.
The issue of temporary housing encampments was referred to the County of Wellington housing symposium, in place of a request that the County study a structured site {{vote:m11}}.
Council asked the County to lead an integrated team doing regular wellness checks at encampments, with City bylaw, paramedic and fire support, and to report quarterly {{vote:m12}}.

debate: Health-sector delegates called the situation a crisis and urged fast action as winter approaches. They asked council to prioritize permanent supportive housing and said finished supportive housing still needs operating funding for support staff. They also wanted the symposium held sooner than early 2024.

Delegates from the chamber of commerce and the poverty task force asked for a coordinated, accountable structure like the London, Ontario model. One delegate said the root problem is inadequate incomes, not only housing supply. Another said the private sector is not best placed to create deeply affordable housing.

Staff and several councillors stressed that property taxes cannot fund all of this alone. Staff said the County is the lead on homelessness services and that provincial and federal funding is needed. Staff said a human rights-based approach does not make the City solely responsible for solving housing.

On the daytime shelter, one councillor wanted to look outside the downtown core. Staff said a broad request for proposals with no location limit would be simpler. Staff also said the current pilot ends December 31, so timing and funding after that are uncertain.

Staff said the four-unit zoning change would likely be caught up in the existing appeal of the comprehensive zoning by-law. On encampments, councillors worried about wraparound services, bylaw and planning requirements, and the symposium agenda. That led to the referral to the symposium.
